# Verified Source Map — OECD Economic Survey Mexico 2022 (Chapter 5B pool)

**Source ID:** MAC-015
**Document title:** OECD Economic Survey Mexico 2022
**Source role:** international_organization
**Document type:** policy_synthesis
**Unit range:** 79–103 (chapter 2, pages 77–101 of the PDF)
**Locators below use PDF page numbers shown at the bottom of each page.**

---

## A. Observed facts (data points, reported by OECD)

- **F1.** Around 47% of the population aged 18–79 held a bank account in Mexico in 2018; Costa Rica 68%, Chile 74%. Locator: p.77, ¶1.
- **F2.** Domestic bank credit to the private sector ≈ 31.4% of GDP in Mexico in 2021; Brazil 38%, Colombia 45%, Costa Rica 55%, Chile 100%. Locator: p.77, ¶2.
- **F3.** SMEs account for 99.7% of all enterprises, 62.6% of private-sector employment, and 35.2% of national gross production (OECD 2018, cited). Locator: p.82, ¶1.
- **F4.** Around 45% of all commercial bank credit to SMEs in 2020 was covered by credit guarantees (Nacional Financiera; Bancomext for exporters). Locator: p.82, ¶1.
- **F5.** "The three largest banks hold more than 50% of total bank assets" (OECD 2019, cited). Banking-sector market concentration "has been flat since 2016." Locator: p.83, ¶1.
- **F6.** Average real GDP per capita of the top three non-oil regions (CDMX, Nuevo León, BCS) is more than 4× that of the bottom three (Chiapas, Oaxaca, Guerrero). Locator: p.81 (Box 2.2), ¶1.
- **F7.** Less than 70% of adults had ≥1 financial product in 2018; little progress since 2015. Rural–urban gap in financial inclusion fell 4 pp (2012–2018) but remained 15 pp. Locator: p.87, ¶1.
- **F8.** Around 39% of adults used informal credit in 2018 (up 5 pp vs 2012); family/friends ≈ 75% of informal credit sources; rural 41% vs urban 37%. Locator: p.92, ¶1.
- **F9.** Practically all adults with a formal job (96%) have at least one financial product; formal employment raises the probability of holding a bank account by 40 pp vs informal. Locator: p.96, ¶2.
- **F10.** Only a fifth of Mexican companies find judicial proceedings simple and fast (INEGI 2016, cited). Locator: p.96, ¶1.
- **F11.** Establishing specialised commercial courts in Estado de México reduced average commercial trial length by 40%. Locator: p.96, ¶1.
- **F12.** Only 29% of adults who contracted a bank account, insurance or credit in 2018 compared alternative products before purchase; Indonesia 83%, France 78%. Locator: p.97, ¶2.
- **F13.** Fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 inhabitants in Mexico are well below the OECD average; most subscriptions are <25 Mbps. Locator: p.100, ¶1–2.
- **F14.** Mobile broadband subscriptions in Mexico are ~20% below the OECD average; mobile costs are in line with the UN 2025 target of ≈2% of avg per-capita income for 1 GB. Locator: p.100, ¶1–2.

---

## B. Author / OECD assertions (assessment, not pure data)

- **A1.** Mexico ranks low in financial inclusion and financial depth relative to OECD and regional peers; "the size of domestic bank credit to the private sector is also low… below what it would be expected on the basis of Mexican's economic fundamentals." Locator: p.77, ¶1–2.
- **A2.** "High interest rate margin… well above what is observed in Chile or other OECD countries, is one of the principal barriers to credit for SMEs." Locator: p.82, ¶2.
- **A3.** High interest margin may signal low competition in banking lending; concentration is "relatively high" in consumer loans and mortgages, "low" in business loans, and "high in the credit card market." Locator: p.83, ¶1.
- **A4.** "Regional economic gaps in Mexico are the largest among OECD countries." Locator: p.81 (Box 2.2), ¶1.
- **A5.** Southern states display poverty rates above 60%. Locator: p.81 (Box 2.2), ¶2.
- **A6.** Reducing information asymmetries would benefit disproportionately the poor (Banerjee & Newman 1993; Cull, Ehrbeck & Holle 2014, cited). Locator: p.93, ¶2.
- **A7.** "An inefficient legal system is also a reason for the low level of bank intermediation in Mexico." Locator: p.96, ¶1.
- **A8.** Financial literacy: Mexico ranks just below the G20 average; performs better than the G20 average in knowledge and attitude; "very poor performance" in paying debt on time, voluntary savings, and comparing products. Locator: p.96, ¶2.
- **A9.** Financial literacy is below national average in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Colima, Zacatecas. Locator: p.96, ¶2.

---

## C. Recommendations / forward-looking guidance (OECD to Mexico)

- **R1.** Implement the 2019 Banxico proposal to expand credit-bureau data sharing; broaden non-traditional data (utility payments, mobile history) to include informal borrowers. Locator: p.84, ¶1.
- **R2.** Develop stock-market and venture-capital ecosystems; create SME-tailored market segments, training, and tutoring (India BSE SME example). Locator: p.86, ¶1.
- **R3.** Embed financial education in compulsory schooling; expand OECD/INFE-style literacy programmes targeting low-income adults. Locator: p.97, ¶1.
- **R4.** Accelerate specialised commercial courts and oral-proceedings reform; strengthen judicial IT infrastructure. Locator: p.96, ¶2.
- **R5.** Extend broadband coverage via "Internet para todos" and CFE Telecomunicaciones; promote passive infrastructure sharing; encourage 5G investment. Locator: p.101, ¶1–2.
- **R6.** Leverage fintechs and open-banking to lower costs of reaching SMEs and microenterprises. Locator: p.83, ¶1; p.84, ¶1.

---

## D. Specific policy actions already implemented (factual reporting)

- **D1.** 2011: National Council for Financial Inclusion (CONAIF); 2016: National Policy for Financial Inclusion, updated 2020. Locator: p.78, ¶2.
- **D2.** Banxico's CoDi digital payment platform; ≈10.8 million activated accounts as of October 2021. Locator: p.80 (Box 2.1).
- **D3.** Banco del Bienestar: 2,700 branches being constructed; suspended lending in August 2021 following a rise in non-performing loans. Locator: p.79 (Box 2.1).
- **D4.** 2019: payroll-linked credit portability across banks. Locator: p.80 (Box 2.1).
- **D5.** 2019: IPO exit tax cut from 30% to 10% — OECD notes "impact has been so far negligible." Locator: p.86, ¶2.
- **D6.** July 2021: capital-requirement weights reduced for SME, consumer, and mortgage credit; new regulation lowered bank reserves on loans to women. Locator: p.80 (Box 2.1); p.87, ¶1.
- **D7.** September 2021: simplified licensing for non-branch retail agent outlets (corresponsales bancarios). Locator: p.80 (Box 2.1).
- **D8.** 2014 telecoms reform improved mobile broadband access, competition, and prices; benefited low-income households. Locator: p.100, ¶2.
- **D9.** "Programa de Cobertura Social 2021-21" extended internet coverage to ≈1 million people, adding 600 thousand users. Locator: p.101, ¶1.
- **D10.** September 2021: National Digital Strategy 2021-24 announced. Locator: p.101, ¶1.

---

## E. Unresolved allegations / interpretive caveats

- **U1.** OECD hedges causal claims: "establishing causality between financial inclusion, growth and inequality is challenging because of limited data availability and because policies aimed at promoting financial inclusion are very recent." Locator: p.78, ¶2.
- **U2.** COFECE (2019) found "anticompetitive practices" among credit bureaus, "two of them belonging to the same economic group"; the report states they have not shared data to "protect their monopolistic position." Locator: p.84, ¶1.
- **U3.** Some large banks have increased market power since the 2014 financial reform (Bátiz-Zuk & Lara Sánchez 2021, cited). Locator: p.83, ¶1.
- **U4.** Reforms' enforcement is uneven: "regional disparities in the implementation and performance of these reforms remain large" (commercial courts). Locator: p.96, ¶1.

---

## F. Limitations, source role, and reopening notes

- **L1.** Time coverage: most data points reference 2018–2021; some pre-2019 outcomes; no post-publication 2022 outcomes included in this excerpt.
- **L2.** Methodological caveat: many cross-country comparisons use different adult-age definitions (Mexico 18–79; others 15+), per Panel-D note on p.77.
- **L3.** Recommendations (Section C) are OECD suggestions, not enacted policy; a stronger model should verify which items have been legislated, funded, and implemented vs. announced.
- **L4.** This extract covers Chapter 2 (financial sector and digital markets). External shocks (inflation, pandemic recovery, commodity effects) referenced in the reading brief are not in this unit range — sections that should be reopened when a stronger model reviews the full survey: Chapter 1 (macroeconomic framework, fiscal stance), Chapter 3 (labour market, informality), and any chapter-level panel on "Sustainable, balanced, and inclusive growth."
- **L5.** Source role caveat: OECD is the cited actor for assessments A1–A9; verify headline numbers (e.g., 31.4% credit-to-GDP, 47% bank-account rate) against CNBV, Banxico, and ENIF micro-data before treating them as adjudicated.
- **L6.** No claim in this map is attributed to the Mexican presidency or to a specific AMLO-era reform decree — the report treats federal policy and institutional design, not the president's personal authorship. No inference about the ruler's motive or incentive was drawn.
- **L7.** Every claim above cites a specific page in the unit range; no claim was carried without a verifiable locator.

---

### Verification notes (factual checker against supplied extract)

- **F1–F2.** p.77 ¶1–2: bank-account share 47% (2018, ages 18–79); bank credit to private sector 31.4% of GDP (2021); Brazil 38%, Colombia 45%, Costa Rica 55%, Chile 100%. Costa Rica 68%, Chile 74% as bank-account shares. ✅
- **F3–F4.** p.82 ¶1: SMEs = 99.7% of enterprises, 62.6% of private employment, 35.2% of national gross production (OECD 2018). Around 45% of SME commercial credit in 2020 covered by credit guarantees from Nacional Financiera and Banco Nacional de Comercio Exterior (exporters). ✅
- **F5.** p.83 ¶1: top three banks hold >50% of total bank assets (OECD 2019); concentration flat since 2016. ✅
- **F6.** p.81 Box 2.2 ¶1: top three non-oil regions (CDMX, Nuevo León, BCS) GDP per capita >4× bottom three (Chiapas, Oaxaca, Guerrero). ✅
- **F7.** p.87 ¶1: <70% of adults had one financial product in 2018; hardly any progress since 2015; rural–urban gap fell 4 pp 2012–2018, still 15 pp (CNBV 2020). ✅
- **F8.** p.92 ¶1: ~39% used informal credit in 2018, +5 pp vs 2012; family/friends ~75% of informal credit sources; rural 41% vs urban 37%. ✅
- **F9.** p.96 ¶2: 96% of adults with formal job have ≥1 financial product; formal employment raises bank-account probability by 40 pp vs informal (Cassimon et al., forthcoming). ✅
- **F10.** p.96 ¶1: only one-fifth of Mexican companies find judicial proceedings simple and fast (INEGI 2016). ✅
- **F11.** p.96 ¶1: specialised commercial courts in Estado de México cut average commercial trial length by 40%. ✅
- **F12.** p.97 ¶2: only 29% of adults who in 2018 contracted a bank account, insurance or credit compared alternatives; Indonesia 83%, France 78%. ✅
- **F13–F14.** p.100 ¶1–2: fixed broadband subscriptions/100 inhabitants well below OECD average, most <25 Mbps; mobile broadband ~20% below OECD average; mobile costs in line with UN target of ~2% of avg per-capita income for 1 GB (4G, 2025). ✅
- **A1.** p.77 ¶1–2 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A2.** p.82 ¶2 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A3.** p.83 ¶1 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A4–A5.** p.81 Box 2.2 ¶1–2 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A6.** p.93 ¶2: reducing information asymmetries benefits the poor (Banerjee & Newman 1993; Cull, Ehrbeck & Holle 2014 cited). ✅
- **A7.** p.96 ¶1 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A8.** p.96 ¶2 verbatim wording present. ✅
- **A9.** p.96 ¶2: regional gap in financial literacy — Chiapas, Oaxaca, Colima, Zacatecas. ✅
- **R1.** p.84 ¶1: implement 2019 Banxico proposal to broaden credit-history sharing; non-traditional data (utility payments, mobile history) for informal borrowers. ✅
- **R2.** p.86 ¶1: develop stock market and venture capital; SME-tailored market segments, training, tutoring; India BSE SME example (launched 2012, 362 listed SMEs as of August 2021). ✅
- **R3.** p.97 ¶1: financial education in compulsory schooling; Peru (ages 4–14, Frisancho 2020), Estonia (primary/basic), Australia (until age 16); PISA results; Banxico Forma launched 2020. ✅
- **R4.** p.96 ¶2: oral proceedings in commercial first instance; specialised commercial courts; National Training Programme for Judges 2017; National Programme on Oral Proceedings. ✅
- **R5.** p.101 ¶1–2: "Internet para todos"; CFE Telecomunicaciones; passive-infrastructure sharing; 5G investment; IT system for sharing passive-infrastructure availability. ✅
- **R6.** p.83 ¶1; p.84 ¶1: fintechs and open-banking approaches for SMEs/microenterprises. ✅
- **D1.** p.78 ¶2: CONAIF 2011; Política Nacional de Inclusión Financiera 2016, updated 2020. ✅
- **D2.** p.80 Box 2.1: CoDi ~10.8 million activated accounts as of October 2021. ✅
- **D3.** p.79 Box 2.1: 2,700 Banco del Bienestar branches; suspended lending August 2021 (rise in non-performing loans). ✅
- **D4.** p.80 Box 2.1: payroll-linked credit portability since 2019. ✅
- **D5.** p.86 ¶2: IPO exit tax cut 30%→10% in 2019; impact "so far negligible." ✅
- **D6.** p.80 Box 2.1; p.87 ¶1: July 2021 capital-requirement weights reduced for SME, consumer, mortgage; July 2021 regulation lowered bank reserves on loans to women. ✅
- **D7.** p.80 Box 2.1: September 2021 simplified authorization for corresponsales bancarios. ✅
- **D8.** p.100 ¶2: 2014 telecoms reform; benefits for low-income households (Ennis, Gonzaga & Pike 2017). ✅
- **D9.** p.101 ¶1: "Programa de Cobertura Social 2021-21" extended coverage to ~1 million people, +600 thousand users. ✅
- **D10.** p.101 ¶1: National Digital Strategy 2021-24 announced in September. ✅
- **U1.** p.78 ¶2 verbatim wording present (Demirguc-Kunt, Klapper and Singer 2017 cited). ✅
- **U2.** p.84 ¶1: COFECE (2019); three credit bureaus; two in same economic group; anticompetitive practices; non-sharing to "protect their monopolistic position." ✅
- **U3.** p.83 ¶1: Bátiz-Zuk and Lara Sánchez 2021 cited. ✅
- **U4.** p.96 ¶1: regional disparities in implementation/performance of commercial-courts reforms ((ITAM) and Gaxiola Calvo 2017; Teplova and Pascual Dapenda 2020). ✅
- **L1–L7.** No factual claims requiring locator verification beyond what's already pinpointed in Sections A–E. ✅

No claims required deletion, unit/period/qualifier rewording, or attribution correction. No omissions were deemed decisive enough for a chapter-lens-only restoration under **VERIFIED ADDITIONS**. No **REOPEN REQUESTS** are raised, since every retained affirmative claim has a precise locator into the supplied extract and matches the cited passage.
